extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered practitioners (patent attorneys/agents), OED counsel, and adjudicators involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to determine rule violations and appropriate sanctions for registered practitioners (attorneys/agents), including procedural service rules, enumerated misconduct provisions, sanctioning factors, and aggravating/mitigating considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to suspend or exclude practitioners (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the USPTO if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for disciplinary action; suspension/exclusion is appropriate where a practitioner has committed gross misconduct, is incompetent, disreputable, or violated Office regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard of proof for both proving violations and asserting affirmative defenses is clear and convincing evidence; adjudicators must apply this burden when assessing claims and defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to timely answer the complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not answer, allegations may be deemed admitted and the tribunal may enter default judgment; procedural notices and deadlines must be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by alternative means/publication when mail returns (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If service by mail cannot be effected because mail is returned, notice may be served by publication (e.g., publication in the Official Gazette) pursuant to § 11.35(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators may find notice adequate when the OED reasonably attempts service at recorded addresses and uses publication as authorized; this affects whether respondent had notice and the propriety of default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify OED of address changes (37 C.F.R. § 11.1l(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must provide written notice to the OED Director of any change in his or her postal address within 30 days of the date of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to update official contact information can affect service and notice; practitioners are responsible for maintaining current contact details with the OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proscribed disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.23(a) proscribes engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the decision include forging USPTO documents, providing misleading information to clients, and concealing abandonment—conduct that supports findings of gross misconduct under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proscribed dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) and § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules proscribe engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (listed under both the Code of Professional Responsibility and the Rules of Professional Conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats fabrication of USPTO documents, false statements about communications with the Office, and collecting fees for non-existent allowances as breaches of these provisions; such conduct supports severe sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.77(c) proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to Office actions, allowing an application to go abandoned, and not informing clients of critical correspondence are concrete examples of neglect under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.84(a)(3) proscribes intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client during the course of a professional relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing an application to go abandoned without client knowledge, forging documents, and causing clients to incur fees and revive proceedings are treated as intentional prejudice/damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to act with reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.103 proscribes failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions such as not replying to Office actions, not pursuing revival, and not responding to client inquiries exemplify breaches of this obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.104(a)(3) proscribes failing to keep a client reasonably informed about the status of their matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing an application's abandonment and failing to notify clients of Office actions or Notices of Abandonment illustrate violations of this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to explain matter sufficiently for client decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.104(b) proscribes failing to explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding their representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not explaining the implications of a Nonpublication Request or failing to advise on options after abandonment exemplify failures under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting and failing to deliver client funds (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.115(d) proscribes failing to promptly deliver to the client any funds that the client is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding or misusing funds (e.g., collecting an 'issue fee' but failing to remit it) and not returning such funds when work isn't performed constitute violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to refund unearned advance fees upon termination (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.116(d) proscribes, upon termination of the practitioner-client relationship, failing to refund any advance payment of fee or expenses that had not been earned or incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a client revokes power of attorney or representation ends and fees remain unearned, practitioners must refund those amounts; failure to do so is grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.804(i) proscribes engaging in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts and omissions that may not fit another specific rule but undermine the practitioner's fitness (e.g., systemic deception, pattern of neglect) fall under this catch-all provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty regarding Nonpublication Request and client consent/consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing a Nonpublication Request, the practitioner must have the client's consent and explain the implications (e.g., inability to monitor application via Public PAIR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to obtain consent or failing to explain consequences (blocking client access to monitoring systems) can be misconduct and an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four sanctioning factors to consider before imposing discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to the client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of any mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators weigh these four factors, with examples in the decision: fiduciary breaches (duty), knowing/intended deception, actual client injury (fees lost, shortened patent life), and limited mitigating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards reference § 9.22 and applied examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors warranting more severe sanctions include dishonest or selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; substantial experience in the practice; refusal or failure to make restitution; bad faith obstruction of disciplinary proceedings (if proved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision identifies several present aggravators: dishonest/selfish motive (pattern of deceit to extract funds), pattern of misconduct over years, multiple violations, substantial experience as an aggravator, and failure to return misappropriated funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA Standards reference and applied examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors may include absence of a prior disciplinary record and other circumstances that may warrant lesser sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes absence of a public disciplinary record as one mitigating factor but found it insufficient to overcome the severity of misconduct given other aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-faith obstruction of disciplinary process as aggravator (when supported by evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad faith obstruction—intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders of the disciplinary agency (e.g., refusing to participate)—is an aggravating factor if demonstrated by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonparticipation may be aggravating, but the tribunal must find the respondent had actual notice or intentionally obstructed; absent proof of notice, nonparticipation alone may not establish this aggravator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria supporting exclusion as sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusion (permanent or time-limited) is appropriate where practitioner violated duties to clients/public/profession, acted knowingly/intentional causing significant injury, engaged in repeated misconduct, and mitigating factors are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies the sanction factors and aggravators to conclude exclusion is appropriate; exclusion deprives the practitioner of eligibility to practice before the Office, subject to reinstatement rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement eligibility and possible conditions (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than at least five years from the effective date of the exclusion; reinstatement, if granted, may be conditioned on restitution to clients among other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions records should note the minimum period before seeking reinstatement and that restitution may be required as a condition for reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner responsibilities upon suspension/exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.58 reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is directed to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 regarding responsibilities in cases of suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must follow procedural responsibilities (e.g., notice to clients, transfer of files) when suspended or excluded; adjudicators may reference § 11.58 for required post-discipline actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to return client files and unearned fees upon termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination or revocation of power of attorney, the practitioner must return client files and refund any unearned fees or expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to return client files or refund unearned fees (as in the facts) is a basis for multiple rule violations and aggravation when assessing sanctions.
